name: Belgian Dubbel
title: Belgian Dubbel: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Belgian dubbel explained: the brown abbey ale with raisin, plum and toffee, how it tastes, how to serve it and Indian dishes to pair.
tagline: A brown abbey ale that tastes of raisins, plums and dark toffee, with a dry, warming finish.
tastes:
Dubbel is the brown ale of the Trappist and abbey tradition. Its modern form took shape at Westmalle in the mid-nineteenth century and spread to other monasteries and then to commercial abbey breweries. The colour and much of the flavour come from dark candi syrup, a caramelised beet sugar that gives raisin, plum and dark toffee notes, along with Munich and some Special B malt.

The Belgian yeast adds dried fruit and a soft spice, so the whole beer tastes something like a fruit cake that has been dried out. It should not be heavy or syrupy. The sugar ferments out, leaving a medium body and a surprisingly dry finish with a gentle warmth from the alcohol. Hops stay low, there only to keep things in balance. Roast is absent; if a dubbel tastes of coffee or burnt toast, it has wandered away from the style. Strength usually sits around six to seven and a half per cent.

profile.look: Deep reddish brown to mahogany, fairly clear, with a thick, long-lasting tan head.
profile.aroma_flavour: Raisin, plum, dark toffee and caramel with a light clove or pepper spice from the yeast, little hop aroma and no roast.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium body, high carbonation, smooth texture and a dry, gently warming finish.
profile.ingredients: Pilsner and Munich malts, a little Special B or aromatic malt, dark candi syrup, low-alpha European hops, a Belgian abbey yeast.

in_india: Dubbel feels made for Indian winter and festival food, with its dried fruit and jaggery-like sweetness. Jaggery makes a natural local swap for candi sugar if you brew one yourself. Mumbai and Bengaluru brewpubs pour it now and then as a seasonal. Serve it cool rather than ice cold, or the fruit and spice stay locked up. It is a slow sipper, better at a Diwali dinner or a Christmas table than at a summer barbecue.

pairings.why: Raisin and toffee notes sit beside the Kashmiri chilli and fennel, and the carbonation lifts the fat.
The meaty jackfruit and whole spices meet the beer's dried fruit for a rich vegetarian main.
Dark sugar and spice in the beer work with the roasted, vinegar-touched pork.
Dried fruit meets dried fruit, and the beer's dry finish stops the pairing from getting heavy.
